# Starter: Requirement Engine

## Setup

```
npm install
npm test        # run the test suite (vitest)
npm run typecheck
```

## The task

`src/types.ts` defines a small requirement-tree language:

- Leaves: `CourseLeaf` (a specific course) and `TagLeaf` (any completed course
  carrying a given tag).
- Internal nodes: `AndNode`, `OrNode`, `NOfMNode` (satisfied by `n` of `m`
  children, backed by **distinct** completed courses -- see the doc comment
  on `NOfMNode` in `types.ts`).

`src/fixtures.ts` has three example requirement trees (a flat breadth
requirement, a 3-level-deep CS major requirement, and a small "global
awareness" N-of-M) plus a handful of example students.

`src/evaluate.ts` exports two functions you need to implement. Both are
currently fully stubbed (they throw `"not implemented"`); each has a doc
comment above it spelling out its contract.

1. **`evaluateRequirement(node, student): EvaluationResult`** -- recursively
   evaluate a `RequirementNode` tree against a student's completed courses.
   Leaves check a specific course or a tag; `and`/`or` combine children the
   obvious way; `n_of_m` is satisfied iff at least `n` of its children are
   backed by *distinct* completed courses (see the doc comment on `NOfMNode`
   in `src/types.ts`). The returned `EvaluationResult` tree should mirror the
   shape of the input, since `getMissingLeaves` (and the tests) walk it.

2. **`getMissingLeaves(result): MissingLeaf[]`** -- given the result of
   `evaluateRequirement`, return the leaves that are still unsatisfied and
   actually relevant (i.e. don't report a losing branch of an OR whose
   sibling already passed, and don't recurse into a child that's already
   satisfied). The contract is spelled out in the doc comment above the
   function in `src/evaluate.ts`.

Run `npm test` -- you're done when all tests in `test/evaluate.test.ts` pass.
Do not change the test file, or the shapes already defined in `src/types.ts`
(adding fields is fine; removing/renaming existing ones will break the
tests).

## Using AI tools

You're welcome to use AI coding tools (Copilot, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor,
etc.) for this exercise -- that's realistic. Please keep a simple log of the
prompts you used (a plain text file or a few bullet points is fine) and be
ready to talk through what you accepted, what you changed, and why. We care
more about your judgment in reviewing/editing AI output than about whether
you used it.
